extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules for the form, content, entitlement, term, and sufficiency of United States letters patent, including how foreign patents affect U.S. patent duration, who may be grantee, the requirements for descriptions and claims, and formal execution issues. Useful for evaluating patent validity and for drafting compliant specifications and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior foreign patent on U.S. patent duration
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute applies where a United States patent corresponds with any invention described in a prior foreign patent; in such cases the U.S. patent may be limited by the foreign patent's term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not apply where the invention was only described (not claimed) in the foreign patent, or where the foreign patent never became operative due to non-compliance with foreign law. If the foreign patent was terminated before the U.S. application was filed the U.S. patent is void ab initio; if the foreign patent terminated while the U.S. application was pending, the U.S. patent is limited by the foreign patent as it would have been if issued on the day applied for. Extensions of a foreign patent (including potential extensions conferred by statute in force when the U.S. application was filed and issued) can affect whether and how the U.S. patent is limited; continuous extensions may extend the limiting effect. Differences in detail do not necessarily avoid the limitation—the true test is whether practicing what is described in the foreign patent would infringe the U.S. patent. A foreign patent for an apparatus does not necessarily limit a U.S. patent for the method, and related/dependent inventions may be affected differently (claims covering inventions patented abroad may expire with the foreign patent while remaining claims remain until U.S. patent expiration). Repeal ab initio of the foreign patent restores the U.S. patent to its full term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term dating and issuance rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms of all United States patents begin at their respective dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent dates cannot be later than nine months after the day on which the respective applications are allowed. Subject to that limitation, patents are dated and issued on the fourth Tuesday after the Patent Office receives the final fees, except where fees are received on Friday, Saturday, or Monday, in which cases they are dated and issued on the fifth Tuesday thereafter. Former statutory provisions about dating were directory, so later issuance does not void a patent for that reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be grantee; assignment and entitlement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The grantee may be the inventor, his assignee, an assignee of an assignee, a guardian or conservator, executor or administrator (in trust for heirs or devisees), a corporation, partnership, or plurality of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor dies after applying but before grant, the patent may be granted in the inventor's name and title vests in executor/administrator or heirs/legatees. If the inventor assigned his inchoate right and requested the patent be granted to the assignee (with the assignment entered on Patent Office records) and then died before grant, courts allow grant to the assignee; statute should receive reasonable construction to avoid divesting an assignee. If an inventor assigns before applying and dies before application, the executor/administrator must make and swear to the application (since assignee cannot apply on the inventor's oath), and the executor/administrator must take the patent in trust for the heirs or devisees—equitable solutions (trusts upon trusts) may be imposed by courts to protect assignee rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content of letters patent (grant, specification, drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent consist of the grant and the specification; drawings that form part of the application are also part of the letters patent and are examined to ascertain the true meaning of terms used in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grant (under the Patent Office seal and signed by the Commissioner) contains a short title and purports to grant to the patentee, heirs or assigns, for seventeen years, the exclusive right to make, use, and vend the invention; each of those three rights is a separate substantive right. Drawings are part of the patent where included and are used to interpret the specification. Grants signed by an Acting or Assistant Commissioner (when lawfully assigned to perform that function) are valid and admissible without proof of title to office. Misnomers in the grant do not invalidate the patent if the patentee can be identified; proper officers may correct mistakes when convinced of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alterations, reissue, and estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly executed letters patent cannot be altered in character by the Commissioner except after a surrender and by means of a reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any alteration made otherwise is void for lack of jurisdiction. However, if the Commissioner actually made an alteration at the patentee's request and a third party relied upon that alteration to their detriment (e.g., embarking in business), the patentee may be estopped from denying the validity of that alteration as to that party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'specification' and its component parts
rubrics_metrics.description: When the statute uses 'specification' without the word 'claim' it covers both the claim and the description; when used with 'claim' it covers the description only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is composed of the description and the claim(s); proper characteristics of specifications are explained via the description and the claims (their required contents and form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description/enablement requirement (full, clear, concise, exact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must set forth the invention and the manner and process of making and using it "in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art or science ... to make and use the same."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For machines, the description must explain the principle and the mode of applying that principle which the inventor believes to be best. Where the essence is location, form, size or other characteristic of means employed, the patent must distinctly specify the peculiarities. Pointing out a form, composition, or construction of a mechanical element when those characteristics are not essential is not a limitation to equivalents. An invention that is an improvement should be read with the prior patent referred to. 'Person skilled in the art' is not limited to the most eminent but includes those whose skill is ordinary in the field. It is sufficient if skilled persons familiar with prior inventions can understand and practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency requirements by subject matter (machine, process, manufacture, composition, design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of inventions have particular description requirements: processes must distinguish and definitely describe new elements; machines must explain principle and mode; manufactures and compositions have proportion and component requirements; designs rely on drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process: must distinguish new elements from old and describe them so as to furnish a clear chart for practical introduction into the art; if enough is indicated to point to a mechanism the process may be sustained even without specific apparatus. Machine: explain principle and best mode. Manufacture/article: where proportion is important, indicate proportions substantially correctly (need not be mathematical) and state how to vary with circumstances. Composition of matter: state component parts and proportions with clearness and precision; should not leave the public to ascertain such facts by experiment. Design: same standards of sufficiency apply, but a verbal description is not necessary if the drawing is sufficiently clear; a written description identifying the "dominant features" can broaden scope beyond the precise drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for errors, omissions, and inventor's lack of theoretical understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is not void because the inventor does not understand the laws of nature causing the invention to work, nor because the inventor or others do not understand all advantages; certain errors and omissions are tolerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors that would be detected and remedied by a person skilled in the art when making specimens or practicing the invention are not fatal. Mistaken statements of immaterial facts, errors relating only to degree of efficiency, or deficient description of some parts' functions are not necessarily sufficient to invalidate a patent. It is not necessary to state every use of the invention, nor every mode or apparatus for a process—describing one workable mode and apparatus with some beneficial result can be enough. However, omission of anything absolutely material to the utility of the invention is a fatal defect unless the omission would naturally be supplied by a skilled person when making or using the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive description and fraudulent intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess of description is not injurious to validity unless redundant matter was introduced with fraudulent intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redundant or superfluous detail does not invalidate a specification absent a showing of fraud in its introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: particularity, function/result limitation, and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must "particularly point out and distinctly claim" the part, improvement, or combination claimed as the invention; a distinct and formal claim is necessary to ascertain scope and the patent grants no exclusive right except to what is thus claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims "measure the invention." A claim covers a process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or a design, and never merely the function or result. A specification may contain a claim for the whole invention and other claims for separate parts or sub-processes; the subject of a claim need not be operative alone. Each claim must satisfy tests of invention (inventive step), novelty, and utility. Matters disclosed but not covered by claim are not within the exclusive grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undisclosed or unclaimed disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions, devices, and improvements disclosed by the specification but not covered by a claim are not secured by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification may describe more than is claimed; anything disclosed yet not claimed is effectively dedicated outside the patentee's exclusive grant and is not part of the monopoly. (Context: the book states this principle and proceeds to emphasize the measuring function of claims.)
